headline_marked: [[Baidu and Lyft begin robotaxi testing]] in London, public service aimed for 2027
headline: Baidu and Lyft begin robotaxi testing in London, public service aimed for 2027
summary: Chinese tech giant Baidu, in partnership with Lyft and Freenow, has started testing its Apollo Go RT6 robotaxis in London with human safety operators. Public availability is targeted for 2027, pending regulatory approval.
details: Chinese tech giant Baidu has commenced testing its Apollo Go RT6 autonomous vehicles in London. This initiative is part of a strategic partnership with Lyft and its European subsidiary, Freenow, with human safety operators present during initial trials.

The testing began on Tuesday, nearly a year after Baidu and Lyft first announced their collaboration to deploy Baidu’s purpose-built robotaxis across key European markets. Lyft acquired Freenow in 2025, gaining a significant foothold in Europe's ride-hailing sector.

London is emerging as a major hub for robotaxi development. Competitors like Waymo also started testing autonomous vehicles in the city in April, while Uber and Wayve plan to launch a robotaxi service with safety operators this year.

Baidu and Freenow by Lyft anticipate inviting the public to hail their robotaxis in 2027. This timeline is subject to regulatory approval and further detailed plans are yet to be announced by the companies.

Currently, dozens of test vehicles are operating within London’s borough of Brent. Discussions are ongoing with local safety and city officials, including Transport for London (TfL) and the Centre for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CCAV).

The UK government is actively developing autonomous vehicle regulations and has opened applications for an AV pilot program. Freenow by Lyft plans to operate a hybrid network, integrating robotaxis with traditional human-driven taxis and private-hire vehicles.

headline_marked: [[Cursor launches India-specific subscription]] for ₹649/month, expanding its third-largest market
headline: Cursor launches India-specific subscription for ₹649/month, expanding its third-largest market
summary: The AI coding startup introduces 'Cursor Start' at roughly $7, significantly lower than its standard $20/month Pro plan, targeting India's vast developer market.
details: AI coding startup Cursor has launched its first country-specific subscription, Cursor Start, in India for ₹649 a month (approximately $7). This new plan is priced well below Cursor’s standard $20-a-month Pro subscription, marking a significant push into one of the world's largest developer markets.

India is already Cursor's third-largest market globally and boasts its highest concentration of power users, with the user base tripling over the past year. This growth, combined with India’s deep pool of software engineering talent, made it the first market for localized pricing.

The country has emerged as a major software developer hub, with GitHub reporting over 27 million developers on its platform in India, second only to the U.S. More than two million developers joined GitHub from India in 2026 alone, highlighting the market's potential.

Cursor Start includes access to Cursor’s Composer 2.5 and Grok 4.5 models, offering higher usage limits than the free tier. It also provides cloud agents, its iOS app, plugins, and Model Context Protocol support, aimed at developers needing more AI-assisted coding capacity.

Unlike the Pro subscription, the India-specific plan does not include access to frontier AI models from providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. It also omits advanced features such as Bugbot, Auto Mode, Automations, and the Cursor SDK, positioning it as a broader access option.

The plan is billed in Indian rupees and supports payments via credit/debit cards and India’s Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Cursor will implement multiple checks to ensure the subscription remains exclusive to individual users within India, deterring VPN access.

Cursor is not alone in tailoring its pricing for India; OpenAI and Anthropic have also rolled out India-specific plans. This reflects a growing trend among global AI companies competing for users in one of the fastest-growing AI markets.

While initially limited to India, Cursor may expand localized pricing to other markets if the model proves successful. OpenAI previously used a similar strategy, launching its sub-$5 ChatGPT Go in India before expanding it globally.

Beyond pricing, Cursor is expanding its physical presence in India with new hires, including its first salesperson and an upcoming leader in Delhi. The company is also establishing a government affairs office and hiring technical customer support staff in major cities like Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, and Mumbai.

The India-specific pricing is designed to be commercially sustainable, not a loss leader, as it leverages Cursor’s own AI models which have lower operating costs. Cursor also sees significant enterprise opportunities in sectors like banking as it expands local sales efforts.
